L0@P0: Do You Need a Receipt? Anonymous Credential Revocation at Continental Scale
L1@P0: via Private Record Certification
L2@P0: Kasra EdalatNejad, Sebastian Faust, Jonas Hofmann, Philipp-Florens Lehwalder, Thomas Schneider
L3@P0: Technical University of Darmstadt, Germany
L4@P0: {edalat, schneider}@encrypto.cs.tu-darmstadt.de,
L5@P0: {sebastian.faust, jonas.hofmann1, philipp-florens.lehwalder}@tu-darmstadt.de
L6@P0: Abstract
L7@P0: A key challenge in digital credential systems is revocation,
L8@P0: that is, the ability to invalidate credentials post-issuance and
L9@P0: verify their status upon presentation. While anonymous credentials enhance privacy over classical credentials (e.g., by
L10@P0: providing unlinkability), they complicate revocation. Existing
L11@P0: revocation schemes for anonymous credentials often suffer
L12@P0: from high client or verifier computation, long delays before
L13@P0: revocation takes effect (e.g., epoch-based settings), or require
L14@P0: updates to all users with each revocation.
L15@P0: We present an efficient, real-time revocation system for anonymous credentials with decentralized revocation authorities
L16@P0: based on a novel primitive called Private Record Certification
L17@P0: (PRC). PRC enables users to obtain a certificate for a record
L18@P0: stored in a server-managed database without the servers learning which record was requested. This primitive is of independent interest, and we construct it by combining techniques
L19@P0: from private information retrieval and secure multi-party computation. Our revocation scheme outsources its computation
L20@P0: to the revocation authorities and has minimal overhead for
L21@P0: clients and verifiers, while ensuring the communication costs
L22@P0: are sublinear in the number of credentials. We build a prototype and demonstrate that our system achieves sub-second
L23@P0: real-time latency for PRC requests, at a scale of over 1 billion
L24@P0: credentials, with an online operational cost of 2.5$ per server
L25@P0: for processing 1 million PRC requests.
L26@P0: 1 Introduction
L27@P0: As governments increasingly move public services online,
L28@P0: electronic identification (eID) is becoming a critical national
L29@P0: infrastructure, serving as the entry point for essential services
L30@P0: like taxes, healthcare, mobility, and education. While eID systems ease administrative burdens for citizens, they also raise
L31@P0: concerns about mass surveillance and the erosion of fundamental rights, such as privacy. European regulations [39] call
L32@P0: for privacy-preserving digital identities that provide strong
L33@P0: authenticity without enabling cross-context linkability. The
L34@P0: European Digital Identity (EUDI) Wallet initiative seeks to
L35@P0: realize these legal requirements, but has major shortcomings
L36@P0: and does not yet provide the demanded privacy guarantees [6].
L37@P0: Anonymous credentials [20, 22, 23] have long been known
L38@P0: to achieve this securely and efficiently and future EUDIW
L39@P0: iterations may adopt anonymous credentials [38].
L40@P0: A central challenge in credential systems is revocation: the
L41@P0: ability to invalidate credentials after issuance, and to verify
L42@P0: a credential’s status during presentation. Privacy-preserving
L43@P0: revocation is not a technical nicety; it is a two-sided safeguard. It protects citizens against identity theft, lost credentials, misuse, and surveillance, while empowering authorities
L44@P0: to enforce accountability in a rights-respecting manner. For instance, suspended driver’s licenses or fraudulent professional
L45@P0: certifications must be revoked without enabling pervasive
L46@P0: profiling of citizens. Privacy can be important for revocation
L47@P0: authorities too, especially when they are law enforcement or
L48@P0: government agencies (e.g., for driver’s licenses). Solutions
L49@P0: that rely on public revocation lists disclose the status of all credentials, exposing unnecessary data and creating legal risks.
L50@P0: Demonstrating that strong privacy and real-time accountability can be achieved simultaneously is essential to counter
L51@P0: the false trade-off between security and civil liberties, which
L52@P0: often stalls adoption of privacy-preserving solutions.
L53@P0: While anonymous credentials offer strong privacy, they
L54@P0: complicate revocation. Existing revocation schemes [5,14,16,
L55@P0: 18, 21, 68, 74, 81] incur expensive client updates per revocation, high verifier costs, or delayed revocation via time-based
L56@P0: epochs, which create “opportunity windows” for abuse of
L57@P0: revoked credentials.
L58@P0: We study the requirements of a practical revocation scheme.
L59@P0: Viable systems should: 1) scale for nation-wide deployment, supporting hundreds of millions of credentials, 2)
L60@P0: support real-time revocation that eliminates the abuse window, and 3) achieve low latency with 4) minimal computational/communication overhead for clients and verifiers, enabling deployment on mobile devices and constrained networks. We align revocation privacy requirements with those
L61@P0-1: of anonymous credential presentations. Since revocation inUSENIX Association 35th USENIX Security Symposium 3179troduces authorities absent from classic credentials, we also
L62@P1: aim to preserve the privacy of the credential status database,
L63@P1: which we call database privacy. In particular, clients must
L64@P1: prove ownership of a credential to learn its revocation status.
L65@P1: We construct a revocation scheme for anonymous credentials that achieves scalability, efficiency, and real-time revocation while maintaining strong privacy guarantees. Clients obtain a non-revocation token from a Revocation Authority (RA)
L66@P1: and present it, along with their credential, to verifiers. We target an on-demand scenario where clients request a new token
L67@P1: immediately before each credential presentation. Therefore,
L68@P1: we must guarantee that non-revocation queries remain unlinkable. We require similar privacy guarantees for RAs as we due
L69@P1: for issuers and verifiers in credential systems. This is needed,
L70@P1: as otherwise the RA could track or discriminate against users
L71@P1: based on their usage patterns, leaked attributes, or revocation
L72@P1: status. To achieve this guarantee, we assume multiple RAs
L73@P1: that share a replicated database in an anytrust setting, where
L74@P1: unlinkability is preserved as long as at least one RA remains
L75@P1: honest. The client does not need to know which one is honest.
L76@P1: This is a realistic model, as in practice, the distributed RA can
L77@P1: be realized as a consortium of different servers, e.g., operated
L78@P1: by different governmental and non-governmental institutions.
L79@P1: As a first step toward a revocation scheme, we introduce a
L80@P1: new primitive called Private Record Certification (PRC) that
L81@P1: enables clients to privately obtain a certificate for a record in a
L82@P1: server-managed database. Concretely, it provides a signature
L83@P1: on a record D[idx] together with its index idx, while hiding
L84@P1: the identity of the client, the index itself, and the record value.
L85@P1: Clients can use this signature in standard zero-knowledge
L86@P1: proofs to demonstrate their record satisfies a desired property.
L87@P1: Beyond revocation, PRC is of independent interest for applications such as privacy-preserving proofs of credit score or
L88@P1: account balance. Our PRC construction combines techniques
L89@P1: from Private Information Retrieval (PIR)[25,33] with Secure
L90@P1: Multi-Party Computation (MPC)[44]. Specifically, we
L91@P1: introduce a novel conversion from Boolean secret sharing
L92@P1: to One-Hot Encoding (OHE) achieving theoretically minimal
L93@P1: client-side complexity, logarithmic in the number of database
L94@P1: records (i.e., the number of bits needed to represent the index
L95@P1: in cleartext). We then combine our secret sharing operations
L96@P1: in a new way with homomorphic commitments, enabling
L97@P1: a seamless transition to asymmetric operations needed for
L98@P1: building a non-revocation token via a (threshold) signature.
L99@P1: Contributions. We summarize our contributions below.
L100@P1: ↭ We introduce Private Record Certification (PRC), a
L101@P1: cryptographic primitive that enables clients to obtain a private
L102@P1: certificate for a record in a server-managed database, along
L103@P1: with formal definitions and security properties.
L104@P1: ↭ We design a PRC scheme with minimal client and verifier cost complexity, and formally prove its security.
L105@P1: ↭ We build a privacy-preserving revocation system for
L106@P1: anonymous credentials, instantiated with our PRC.
L107@P1: ↭ We implement and evaluate our PRC construction,
L108@P1: demonstrating that our revocation system achieves real-time
L109@P1: revocation while scaling to billions of credentials with subsecond latency for revocation status lookups. Our solution is
L110@P1: also cost-efficient: the online operation costs per PRC server
L111@P1: for one million queries are only 2.5$, based on AWS pricing.
L112@P1: 1.1 Technical Overview
L113@P1: We provide a high-level technical overview of our solution
L114@P1: next. We build a revocation scheme where a decentralized
L115@P1: RA keeps a private status list D, such that D[idx] → {0,1} is
L116@P1: the validity status of the credential with a private index idx
L117@P1: (see §6). When clients want to present one of their credentials,
L118@P1: they need to prove that D[idx]= 1, while 1) binding idx to the
L119@P1: index embedded in their credential and 2) hiding idx to ensure
L120@P1: unlinkability. To achieve this goal, we define a primitive called
L121@P1: PRC that allows the client to interact with RAs to privately
L122@P1: obtain a signed commitment linking (idx,D[idx]), also called
L123@P1: a non-revocation token. When clients present their credential,
L124@P1: they present a non-revocation token and use zero-knowledge
L125@P1: proofs to link the index in the credential to the token (i.e.,
L126@P1: proof of discrete log equality) and reveal the record value
L127@P1: D[idx]= 1. The verifier validates a) the credential presentation, b) the RA’s signature on the token, and c) the ZK-proof
L128@P1: proving the token corresponds to the credential. Since PRC
L129@P1: provides unforgeability, the verifier can be certain that the
L130@P1: revealed revocation status belongs to presented credential.
L131@P1: PRC. We define and construct a PRC scheme in §5, where
L132@P1: given a private index, the PRC servers compute and then sign
L133@P1: a commitment to (D[idx],idx) that binds an index to its record
L134@P1: value. We design a PRC protocol in the following steps: 1)
L135@P1: the client Boolean secret shares its index among PRC servers.
L136@P1: 2) the servers convert their boolean shares of idx to arithmetic
L137@P1: shares and compute arithmetic shares of the database record
L138@P1: D[idx]. This step has a similar nature as PIR, and we design
L139@P1: a custom optimized variant of it, which we discuss below. 3)
L140@P1: Each server commits to its arithmetic share of the index and
L141@P1: record value via a homomorphic commitment like Pedersen.
L142@P1: 4) The PRC servers aggregate the homomorphic commitment.
L143@P1: As we deliberately choose the same group order between our
L144@P1: commitment and arithmetic sharing, this aggregation acts as a
L145@P1: secret reconstruction without revealing the cleartext values to
L146@P1: PRC servers. 5) The PRC servers sign the final commitment.
L147@P1: We extend this scheme in §5.4 to achieve database privacy,
L148@P1: by requiring clients to add a ZK-proof (similar to the proof
L149@P1: used for presenting a non-revocation token) showing that they
L150@P1: have an authorization for the requested index.
L151@P1: Record retrieval. In step 2) of our PRC scheme, the PRC
